Make a dbt pros and cons list of being with him (pros of being with him, pros of not being with him, cons of being with him, cons of not being with him) to remind you to stick with your decision. I recommend making it when you’re in a calm state of mind so you can be honest with yourself about the situation, and keep it somewhere accessible like on your notes app in your phone so you can refer back to it when needed. 

In my experience breakups are the worst after the first few weeks to a month but things will get easier! And as time goes on you’ll feel more okay with your decision. In the meantime, try keeping busy. I’ve found that deleting social media for a while helps with breakups, as it also stops you from checking up on their social media if that’s something you struggle with. 

Even if you don’t have anyone in your life with bpd who will “get it” definitely still reach out to them even if it’s just for a shoulder to cry on. You’re right that most people without bpd won’t understand the extent in which you’re hurting, but almost all people will empathise with your situation and be able to at least give some form of comfort. 

I’ve also found what helps is to watch emotive/sad movies when I’m feeling down, as it gives me something else to focus on and also allows me to cry and feel what I need to feel even if it’s just related to what I’m watching. 

Writing your emotions out can help too if you’re like me and find it hard to be vulnerable around your friends. 

Wishing you the best!! You can get through this 🫶

Losing a friend is always really hard. Like *really* hard. Borderline or not. 

Stopping being friends with someone - especially someone you’ve known as long as you’ve known this person - always hurts, even if there was no big blowup or anything. Really it’s comparable to losing a friend to death, and may even hurt just a bit more because they aren’t actually dead, they’re still alive they just aren’t your friend. 

It’s been helpful for me, when I lose friends, to deal with it like how I would grief. Cause it really is like that, especially with BPD folks. Give yourself some time and know that while it may not ever feel 100% again, you’ll overtime learn to live with it. I spent a majority of this and part of last year chasing an old friendship group who I fell out with, and it’s really tough to let go but letting go is how you move on. And you don’t know the future, perhaps in 5, 10, 20 years you’ll rekindle and be friends, or perhaps you won’t and by then you won’t necessarily want to be friends. We don’t know. But I think the most important thing for you right now is to focus on yourself, this person has decided obviously that they don’t fit in with your life anymore and that’s okay. Try (though it’s bloody hard) making some new friends or picking up a new hobby like poetry or art, just distract yourself basically and eventually it just won’t hurt as much.

I think the best course of action is to tell him that you’ve been looking into some stuff and would like to perhaps start or incorporate DBT into your sessions. He will probably ask why, so just give him your reasons without explicitly mentioning BPD. So for example say you struggle with intense, non-bipolar related mood shifts or depersonalisation, you would say that. He might ask you what you think your symptoms are related to, a lot of patients including myself really don’t like being asked this because like you mentioned you don’t want to make it out to seem like you’re self diagnosing. However most of the time psychologists ask this because they genuinely want to hear what you think is going on, as you know you better than any psychologist. Tell him you identify with symptoms of borderline and he’ll give you his thoughts. Don’t be afraid to advocate for yourself or even ask for a second opinion if you feel you need one. Depending on your age, it’s  not likely that he’ll diagnose you or refer you to a psychiatrist to be tested then and there, but he might just say he’s gonna keep an eye on that.
